learn.heading: Learn
learn.intro: How inflation is measured and how to read a release, with examples from the latest data.

mom.title: Monthly change (MoM)
mom.body: The percentage change in the price index from one month to the next.

yoy.title: 12-month change
yoy.body: The change against the same month a year earlier. This is the headline number in the news. It compounds the last 12 monthly changes: (1+m₁)(1+m₂)…(1+m₁₂) − 1.
yoy.example: Over the 12 months to {{period}}, prices rose {{value}}.

ytd.title: Year to date
ytd.body: The accumulated change since December of the previous year.

sa.title: Seasonal adjustment
sa.body: Some prices move with the calendar: school fees in February, food after harvests. Seasonal adjustment removes these regular patterns so a monthly change can be read as a trend.

saar.title: Annualized rate (SAAR)
saar.body: A seasonally adjusted 3- or 6-month change, expressed as if it lasted a year. It shows turning points before the 12-month rate does, at the cost of more noise.

core.title: Core inflation
core.body: Measures that strip out volatile prices to show the underlying trend. Each one does it differently: excluding items, trimming the extremes or reweighting by volatility. The central bank watches their average.
core.example: The core average is {{value}} over 12 months.

contribution.title: Contribution
contribution.body: How many percentage points of the headline change came from a component: roughly its weight times its own change. Contributions add up to the headline.

diffusion.title: Diffusion
diffusion.body: The share of items whose prices rose in the month. A high share means increases are widespread, not concentrated in a few items.

band.title: Target and tolerance band
band.body: Brazil's target is 3% with a tolerance of ±1.5 pp. Since 2025 the target is continuous: it counts as missed when the 12-month rate stays outside the band for 6 consecutive months, and the central bank must explain why in an open letter.
band.example: The 12-month rate is {{value}} away from the target.

surprise.title: Surprise
surprise.body: The actual number minus what was expected before the release, in percentage points. We use the last survey published before release day.
surprise.example: This release came in {{value}} versus the expectation.

base.title: Base effect
base.body: Next month's 12-month rate depends on which month leaves the 12-month window. If the new print is bigger than the one dropping out, the 12-month rate rises, whatever the trend.
base.example: At the next release, {{period}} ({{value}}) drops out.

real.title: Real interest rate (ex-ante)
real.body: The policy rate after expected inflation: (1 + rate) / (1 + expected inflation) − 1. It shows how tight monetary policy really is.

vintage.title: Vintage
vintage.body: The value as first published at a release, before any revision. Keeping vintages makes surprises and revisions traceable.

howTo.title: How to read an inflation release
steps: Start with the monthly change and compare it with the expectation: was it a surprise?
Look at the 12-month rate and its distance from the target.
Check what drove the month: which groups and items contributed most?
Look past the noise: are core measures and diffusion moving the same way?
Check momentum: are the 3- and 6-month annualized rates above or below the 12-month rate?
Look ahead: which month drops out of the 12-month window next?

methodology.heading: Methodology and sources
methodology.intro: Every number on this site comes from official sources and passes a set of checks before it is published. If any check fails, nothing is published and the previous version stays online.

sourcesBr.ibge: IBGE (Instituto Brasileiro de Geografia e Estatística): IPCA and IPCA-15, via the SIDRA API (tables 7060, 1419, 1737 and 7062) and the release calendar.
sourcesBr.sgs: Banco Central do Brasil, SGS time series: core measures, diffusion, free and administered prices, services, Selic target, USD/BRL.
sourcesBr.focus: Banco Central do Brasil, Focus market survey (Olinda API): monthly, 12-month and year-end IPCA expectations.

methods: 12-month and year-to-date changes compound monthly changes.
Contributions are weight × change; over 12 months they are chain-linked so they add up to the 12-month rate.
Annualized rates use an index seasonally adjusted with X-13ARIMA-SEATS (US Census Bureau); the latest 12 months are revisable.
The expected value for a release is the latest survey dated before release day.
Our numbers must match the published ones within 0.01 pp (one unit in the last published digit).
limits: No IPCA-15 expectation is published by the Focus survey.
English names for IBGE items are our own translation.
Core 12-month rates are compounded from the BCB's monthly core series.
methodology.docs: Full formulas and source codes are in the project's documentation on GitHub.
